summary: A 1974 proposal for extending the ARPANET host-to-host protocol so that hosts can detect and recover from lost messages. It builds on earlier discussion in RFC 534, RFC 516, RFC 512, RFC 492 and RFC 467.

plainLanguage.summary: If a letter goes missing in the mail, you want to notice and ask for it again. This note suggests a way for computers on the early network to do that.

questions: how did arpanet recover lost messages
host to host protocol error recovery
subtitle: Detecting lost messages in ARPANET and recovering with retransmission

tldr.problem: The original Host-to-Host protocol could not detect lost messages, leading to inconsistent connection states and the frustrating 'lost allocate' problem where one side thought data could be sent and the other did not.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol adds a four-bit Message Sequence Number (MSN) to each message and an eight-bit Link Resynch Number (LRN) to detect losses and resynchronize. When loss is detected, hosts exchange control messages to either recover by retransmitting or negotiate whether to accept the loss and continue.
tldr.outcome: Type B hosts can detect and recover from message loss while remaining compatible with older Type A hosts that do not implement the protocol.

today: RFC 663 proposed a lost message detection and recovery protocol for the ARPANET Host-to-Host protocol in 1974. The fundamental ideas of sequence numbering and retransmission with resynchronization have become standard in modern reliable transport protocols like TCP, though the specific protocol described here is no longer in use.

sections.title: Lost Message Detection and Recovery
sections.content:
RFC 663 proposes an extension to the ARPANET Host-to-Host protocol to detect messages lost in transmission and provide procedures for recovery. The problem it addresses is significant: when a message is lost, especially on a control link, the two communicating hosts can end up in inconsistent states.

A famous symptom is the "lost allocate" problem described in earlier RFCs. The receiving host thinks the sending host has buffer allocation to send more data. The sending host, having lost the allocation message, thinks it has no allocation and cannot send. The connection becomes paralyzed.

Previous proposals were to mask the symptoms by resynchronizing. This RFC instead proposes solving the fundamental problem: detecting lost messages and recovering from them.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages sometimes got lost on the early network. When that happened, the two computers would disagree about what was sent, and neither could fix it. This RFC adds a way to notice and recover.

sections.title: Core Design Principles
sections.content:
The protocol uses two new fields. The Message Sequence Number (MSN) is a four-bit field that counts up from 1 to 15 then back to 1. By examining this sequence, the receiver can detect that a message with a sequence number is missing. The second field is the Link Resynch Number (LRN), an eight-bit field used to resynchronize communication after an error.

Messages lost are detected by gaps in the MSN sequence. For example, if messages 1, 2, 3, 5 arrive, message 4 was lost. The receiver increments its LRN, sends a control message reporting the loss, and the sender either retransmits the lost messages on the new LRN or informs the receiver it cannot.

The protocol is designed to be compatible with older hosts that do not implement these features. Type A hosts (old implementations) always set MSN and LRN to zero. Type B hosts (new implementations) use the protocol only when communicating with other Type B hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender numbers each message: 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. If the receiver sees 1, 2, 4 instead of 1, 2, 3, 4, it knows message 3 got lost and asks for it again.

sections.title: Detection and Control Messages
sections.content:
When a receiver detects lost messages, it sends an LMR (Lost Message from Receiver) control message specifying the sequence number of the first missing message and the new LRN value.

The sender has several options. It can retransmit starting from the specified message number on the new LRN. Or, if the sending host has already discarded those messages and cannot retransmit, it sends an LMS (Lost Message from Sender) message asking whether the receiver will accept the loss. The receiver can either close the connection or send an LMA (Loss of Messages Acceptable) message to indicate it will continue without those messages.

To handle the case where the last control message itself is lost, the protocol specifies that after a control message, if the sender receives no reply within a timeout, it may retransmit using the same sequence number. The receiver ignores duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: When the receiver notices a gap, it tells the sender which message is missing. The sender can send it again, or if it does not have it anymore, ask if the receiver will keep going anyway.

sections.title: Connection Management and Compatibility
sections.content:
For control link errors (which cannot accept loss), if the sender cannot retransmit, it must send a Reset command, effectively breaking the connection and forcing reinitialization. The protocol defines new commands for closing connections between Type B hosts: CLS2 (a close that includes the sender's LRN and MSN values) and ECLS (Error Close, used for connections broken by irrecoverable errors).

To prevent buffer overflow and ensure no more than 15 messages are in flight at once, the protocol includes a status exchange mechanism with RSS/RSR query messages and SFS/SFR status replies, allowing senders to learn which messages were received and safely discard buffered copies.

Type B hosts detect Type A hosts by observing zero MSN values and simulate Type A behavior for those connections. The protocol is flexible, allowing hosts to implement only loss detection without recovery, or full recovery. Different implementations can interoperate as long as they follow the basic protocol rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol shows how to properly close connections, how to ask which messages got through so old copies can be deleted, and how old and new systems can talk to each other by having the new ones adjust their behavior.
